passage.en:
Haritbhumi has 25 seats. The candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even with less than 50 per cent. Party A polled 40 per cent, Party B 35 and Party C 25, and Party A formed the government.

Ratnadweep also has 25 seats. To win, a candidate needs more than 50 per cent, or the top two compete again. Party X polled 45 per cent, Party Y 40 and Party Z 15. In Round 2, Party Y won with 55 per cent and formed the government.

Swarnalok has 100 seats on a nationwide list, and voters vote for a party. Parties M, N, O and P polled 40, 35, 15 and 10 per cent, and received 40, 35, 15 and 10 seats.

stem.en: In which country did a party form the government with less than half of the votes?

text.en: Ratnadweep, where Party Y polled 55 per cent in Round 2
Haritbhumi, with Party A on 40 per cent
Swarnalok, where four parties shared power by votes
None, as every government there had over half of the votes

explanation.en: Party A formed the government of Haritbhumi with 40 per cent of the votes. Party Y had 55 per cent in Round 2, and in Swarnalok no single party formed the government.

hints.en: Look for a party that formed the government with a share below 50 per cent.

stem.en: Party X polled the most votes in Ratnadweep's first round. Why did it not form the government?

text.en: It had not won more than half of the 25 seats in the country.
Its votes were shared in proportion among the other parties.
It had less than 50 per cent, so a second round was held.
A third party on 15 per cent had to be added to its votes.

explanation.en: Ratnadweep's rule asks for more than 50 per cent of the votes. Party X had 45 per cent, so the top two competed again, and Party Y won that round with 55 per cent.

hints.en: Is the rule 'most votes' or 'more than half'?

stem.en: In Swarnalok, Party O polled 15 per cent of the votes. How many seats did it receive?

text.en: No seats, because it was not the largest party
25 seats, as in the other two countries
One seat, because every party gets one seat

explanation.en: Seats in Swarnalok are allotted in proportion to the votes, so 15 per cent of the votes becomes 15 of the 100 seats.

prompt.en: Using the three countries, explain how a country's rule decides who wins. Name the rule each country uses.

label.en: Haritbhumi uses First Past The Post: the most votes in each constituency wins the seat

clue.en: Each of its 25 seats is decided on its own, in one constituency, by a vote for a person.

clue.en: Haritbhumi needs the most votes; Ratnadweep needs more than half, and runs a second round when nobody gets it.

label.en: The rule a country uses decides how votes become seats

level1.en: What decides how votes turn into seats in each country?

clue.en: Each country counts in its own way: per constituency, in two rounds, or by share of all the votes.

level2Template.en: Results differ because the ___ decides how votes become seats.

text.en: A country's rule decides how votes become seats, so the rule shapes who wins.
Haritbhumi uses First Past The Post: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even with less than half.
Ratnadweep uses the majority system: a candidate needs more than 50 per cent. If nobody has it, the top two compete again, so Party X led Round 1 and still lost.
Swarnalok uses proportional representation: voters vote for a party, and seats follow each party's share of the votes.
So the rule matters as much as the votes, because it decides how votes turn into seats and government.

explanation.en: Haritbhumi counts each constituency and gives the seat to the leader. Ratnadweep asks for more than half of the votes, with a second round. Swarnalok shares seats in proportion to votes.

hints.en: For each country, ask what a winner needs.
